column1: Reconstruct the copy principle and the missing shade of blue (Enquiry 2; Treatise 1.1.1).
column2:
Aim: every simple idea is copied from a simple impression.
Premises: complex ideas resolve into simple ones; every simple idea examined is "copied from a similar impression" (EHU 2.6); a blind man has no ideas of colour (EHU 2.7); impressions come first, so "our impressions are the causes of our ideas, not our ideas of our impressions" (T 1.1.1.8).
Conclusion: all ideas copy impressions. The test: "from what impression is that supposed idea derived?" (EHU 2.9).
Counter-example: the missing shade of blue, which Hume calls "so singular" that the maxim stands (EHU 2.8).
Objection: an inductive rule with an admitted exception cannot show a disputed idea empty; Reid, Bennett.
Reply (the literature's): the shade is built from neighbouring impressions (Garrett); Hume mostly uses the test to find an idea's content.

column1: Reconstruct Hume's fork: relations of ideas and matters of fact (Enquiry 4.1–2; Treatise 1.3.1).
column2:
Aim: every object of reasoning is a relation of ideas or a matter of fact.
Premises: relations of ideas (geometry, algebra, arithmetic) are "discoverable by the mere operation of thought" (EHU 4.1); "The contrary of every matter of fact is still possible; because it can never imply a contradiction" (EHU 4.2); the conceivable is never refuted by demonstration.
Conclusion: no matter of fact can be proved a priori. Applied to libraries: "Commit it then to the flames" (EHU 12.34).
Objections: the fork fails its own test, a charge later pressed against Ayer's verification principle; Kant's synthetic a priori; Quine denies any sharp line.
Reply (the literature's): the fork is a finding of the science of man, open to revision; Kant's examples may be analytic or not a priori; Quine removes the line both relied on.

column1: Reconstruct the problem of induction (Enquiry 4.14–23; Treatise 1.3.6).
column2:
Aim: no argument shows the unobserved will resemble the observed.
Premises: expecting bread to nourish again is "an inference, which wants to be explained" (EHU 4.16); reasoning is demonstrative or probable (EHU 4.18); not demonstrative, since "it implies no contradiction, that the course of nature may change" (EHU 4.18); a probable argument presupposes the future resembles the past, so "must be evidently going in a circle" (EHU 4.19).
Conclusion: "it is not reasoning which engages us to suppose the past resembling the future" (EHU 4.23).
Objection: Strawson: asking whether induction is reasonable is like asking whether the law is legal; Popper: science needs only deduction.
Reply (the literature's): we can still ask whether such beliefs tend to be true (Salmon); trusting tested theories is inductive; Goodman's grue deepens the problem.

column1: Reconstruct custom and belief, the sceptical solution (Enquiry 5; Treatise 1.3.7–8).
column2:
Aim: custom carries us from past to future; belief is a manner of conception.
Premises: the inference is not reasoning (Argument 3); after constant conjunction "we are determined by custom alone to expect the one from the appearance of the other" (EHU 5.5); custom explains why a hundred instances move us, one not.
Conclusion: "Custom, then, is the great guide of human life" (EHU 5.6). An added idea could be believed at will, so belief is a feeling: "A lively idea related to or associated with a present impression" (T 1.3.7.5).
Objections: Reid: vivid novels are not believed; and custom gives no warrant beyond a dog's.
Reply: Hume's own: romance and true history differ in liveliness (T 1.3.7.8). The literature's (Loeb, Garrett): general rules (T 1.3.13, 1.3.15) let some customs correct others.

column1: Reconstruct the argument about the idea of necessary connexion (Enquiry 7; Treatise 1.3.14).
column2:
Aim: the idea of necessary connexion is copied from a feeling in the mind.
Premises: ideas copy impressions; in billiards, impulse followed by motion "is the whole that appears to the outward senses" (EHU 7.6); nor does the will show power (EHU 7.10); events seem "conjoined, but never connected" (EHU 7.26); after repetition, habit makes the mind expect the attendant (EHU 7.28).
Conclusion: the idea is copied from that customary transition; "necessity is something, that exists in the mind, not in objects" (T 1.3.14.22).
Objections: Reid: day and night are constantly conjoined without causing each other. The New Hume (Wright, Craig, G. Strawson): Hume believed in real but unknown powers.
Reply (the literature's): the rules of T 1.3.15 find the common cause; Winkler, Blackburn, Millican: the copy principle leaves such powers no content. Open.

column1: Reconstruct the reconciling project of liberty and necessity (Enquiry 8).
column2:
Aim: the free-will dispute "has hitherto turned merely upon words" (EHU 8.3).
Premises: necessity is constant conjunction plus the mind's inference (Argument 5); "The same motives always produce the same actions" (EHU 8.7); everyone reasons from motive to action, as a prisoner weighs his gaoler with the walls (EHU 8.19); liberty can only mean "a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will" (EHU 8.23), which all not in chains have.
Conclusion: liberty and necessity are compatible. Blame even needs necessity, through lasting character (EHU 8.29).
Objection: Reid and Kant: this leaves open whether one could have willed otherwise; van Inwagen's consequence argument.
Reply: Hume's own: an undetermined act would be chance (EHU 8.25). The literature's: P. F. Strawson's reactive attitudes; Frankfurt denies that responsibility needs alternatives.

column1: Reconstruct the argument about belief in body (Treatise 1.4.2; Enquiry 12.7–16).
column2:
Aim: belief in continued, distinct bodies comes from the imagination; the philosophers' double existence has no footing.
Premises: the senses cannot show continued or distinct existence (T 1.4.2.3–4); nor does reason, since children and peasants hold the belief without argument (T 1.4.2.14); the imagination works on constancy and coherence and feigns continued existence (T 1.4.2.18–20); pressing an eye shows perceptions depend on our organs, so philosophers posit objects behind them, supported by neither reason nor imagination.
Conclusion: that system is "the monstrous offspring of two principles, which are contrary to each other" (T 1.4.2.52).
Objection: Reid: the shared "ideal theory" is the error; we perceive the table itself. Austin attacks EHU 12.9.
Reply: Hume's own: he asks only what causes a belief "we must take for granted in all our reasonings" (T 1.4.2.1).

column1: Reconstruct the bundle theory and the Appendix second thoughts (Treatise 1.4.6; Appendix 10–21).
column2:
Aim: there is no idea of a simple, persisting self; the Appendix finds the positive account fails.
Premises: every real idea comes from one impression; an impression of self would have to last unchanged (T 1.4.6.2); none does; introspection always stumbles "on some particular perception or other" (T 1.4.6.3).
Conclusion: we are "nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions" (T 1.4.6.4); identity is a fiction of the imagination (T 1.4.6.15).
Appendix: "I find myself involv'd in such a labyrinth" (T App.10), with two principles he "cannot render consistent" (T App.21). Its problem is disputed (Garrett; G. Strawson).
Objection: Butler: memory presupposes identity; Reid: perceptions need a perceiver.
Reply (the literature's): introspection reports only perceptions; memory "does not so much produce as discover personal identity" (T 1.4.6.20); Parfit defends a bundle view.

column1: Reconstruct the case for mitigated scepticism (Enquiry 12.21–34; Treatise 1.4.7).
column2:
Aim: the right response to the sceptical results is neither total doubt nor dogmatism.
Premises: the objections of Sections 4–7 are unanswerable (EHU 12.22); total doubt cannot be held: "Nature is always too strong for principle" (EHU 12.23); if held, all human life would perish; there remain "a degree of doubt, and caution, and modesty" (EHU 12.24) and limits on enquiry (EHU 12.25).
Conclusion: mitigated scepticism; philosophy is common life "methodized and corrected" (EHU 12.25).
Objection: Reid: either the arguments are sound and we must doubt all, or the theory of ideas is wrong. And superstition is a lively propensity too.
Reply: Hume's own: he denies that a belief must be proved or abandoned. The literature's: the Title Principle (T 1.4.7.11) and general rules filter superstition (Garrett); Kemp Smith, Popkin and Fogelin dispute the balance.

column1: Reconstruct the argument of "Of miracles" (Enquiry 10).
column2:
Aim: testimony never makes belief in a miracle reasonable, least as a religion's foundation; miracles are not called impossible.
Premises: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence" (EHU 10.4); trust in testimony rests on experience; "A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature" (EHU 10.12), and uniform experience of the laws is a full proof against it.
Conclusion: testimony establishes a miracle only if "its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish" (EHU 10.13). Part 2: in fact the condition is never met.
Objections: Campbell: circular, since laws rest on testimony; Price: the lottery report; Earman: independent witnesses can make the improbable probable.
Reply (the literature's): Fogelin and Millican read the maxim as comparative probability; eight days of darkness could be believed (EHU 10.36).

column1: Reconstruct the design argument and Philo's objections (Dialogues 2–8; Enquiry 11).
column2:
Aim (Cleanthes): God exists and resembles a human mind.
Premises: the world is "nothing but one great machine" (DNR 2.5); its fit of means to ends resembles human contrivance; like effects have like causes.
Conclusion: "the Author of Nature is somewhat similar to the mind of man" (DNR 2.5).
Philo: weak analogy; a unique universe (DNR 2.24); a designing mind needs a cause too (DNR 4.9); the cause may be finite or plural, "some infant deity" (DNR 5.12); the world resembles "an animal or a vegetable" (DNR 7.3); Epicurean matter could explain order (DNR 8).
Objection: Cleanthes' voice in the clouds and the eye (DNR 3.2, 3.7); Reid: design is read by a first principle.
Reply: Philo's own (DNR 12.33): the cause "probably bear some remote analogy to human intelligence," affecting nothing in life.

column1: Reconstruct the problem of evil (Dialogues 10–11).
column2:
Aim: if God's goodness must be read off the world, misery blocks the inference; and the first causes are probably neither good nor malicious.
Premises: on Cleanthes' method God's attributes come from the world alone; misery mixes with good; it is not what a powerful, wise, benevolent being would lead us to expect (DNR 11.4); "The consistence is not absolutely denied, only the inference" (DNR 11.4).
Conclusion: no ground for inferring infinite goodness. Of four hypotheses, "The fourth, therefore, seems by far the most probable" (DNR 11.15).
Objection: theodicy: Demea's future state (DNR 10.29), Leibniz's best world, Plantinga's free-will defence, Wykstra's sceptical theism.
Reply: Philo's own: he concedes the logical problem (DNR 10.35), but "A mere possible compatibility is not sufficient." Free will leaves the four natural circumstances untouched; sceptical theism costs the design argument.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that reason is the slave of the passions (Treatise 2.3.3).
column2:
Aim: reason alone never moves action and never opposes a passion.
Premises: reason is demonstrative or causal (T 2.3.3.2); demonstration concerns ideas, not realities; causal reasoning: "the impulse arises not from reason, but is only directed by it" (T 2.3.3.3); only a contrary impulse can oppose an impulse (T 2.3.3.4).
Conclusion: "Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions" (T 2.3.3.4). Passions represent nothing: "'Tis not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger" (T 2.3.3.6).
Objection: Price: moral perception motivates; Kant: morality needs categorical imperatives; Korsgaard: instrumental reason is itself a requirement.
Reply: the thesis is about motivation; reason corrects beliefs and means (T 2.3.3.7). Michael Smith's direction of fit restates it; the internal/external reasons dispute (Williams) is open.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that moral distinctions are not derived from reason, and the is/ought passage (Treatise 3.1.1).
column2:
Aim: reason does not tell virtue from vice; morality is felt.
Premises: (a) "Morals excite passions, and produce or prevent actions" (T 3.1.1.6), and reason alone cannot; (b) "Reason is the discovery of truth or falshood" (T 3.1.1.9), and passions and actions agree with nothing; (c) a sapling killing its parent oak is not guilty (T 3.1.1.24), and in a murder "The vice entirely escapes you" until you feel disapprobation (T 3.1.1.26).
Conclusion: moral rules are not conclusions of reason. Coda: the step from is to ought needs explaining (T 3.1.1.27).
Objections: externalists (Brink): amoralists show judgment need not motivate; Searle derives ought from promising; MacIntyre: Hume intended no ban.
Reply (the literature's): Hume needs only characteristic motivation; Hare: Searle adds an evaluative premise; the passage demands explanation; it is not Moore's naturalistic fallacy.

column1: Reconstruct justice as an artificial virtue and the circle in its motive (Treatise 3.2.1–2; EPM 3).
column2:
Aim: justice rests on convention and is approved for its usefulness.
Premises: an act is virtuous only from a motive other than regard to its virtue (T 3.2.1.4); before convention, self-interest, public concern and private benevolence all fail to make me repay a loan (T 3.2.1.10–13); leaving only regard to justice, "an evident sophistry and reasoning in a circle" (T 3.2.1.17).
Conclusion: justice "arises artificially, tho' necessarily from education, and human conventions" (T 3.2.1.17): a convention without promise, like two men rowing (T 3.2.2.10). Interest founds it; sympathy with public interest approves it (T 3.2.2.24).
Objection: Reid: justice is natural, and regard to duty can be a first motive; also, convention needs prior trust.
Reply: Hume's own: the rules are "not arbitrary" (T 3.2.1.19). The literature's: the convention grows gradually, as Lewis models.

column1: Reconstruct the sensible knave (EPM 9.22–25).
column2:
Aim: virtue serves our interest, except perhaps in justice.
Premises: society needs a general regard to property; one injustice can enrich without breaching the social union (EPM 9.22); "honesty is the best policy, may be a good general rule; but is liable to many exceptions" (EPM 9.22).
Conclusion (the knave's): keep the rule and exploit every exception.
Hume's answer: if the knave needs an answer, "it will be a little difficult to find any" (EPM 9.23); the honest keep "Inward peace of mind, consciousness of integrity" (EPM 9.23); knaves are usually caught and are "the greatest dupes" (EPM 9.24–25).
Objection: it convinces only those needing no answer; Gauthier: interest-based justice cannot call the knave irrational.
Reply: by Argument 13 no argument motivates without a passion; Gauthier's constrained maximizer supports the claim that knaves get caught.

column1: What is the difference between impressions and ideas?
column2: Hume's word for any content of the mind is "perception." "All the perceptions of the human mind resolve themselves into two distinct kinds, which I shall call Impressions and Ideas" (T 1.1.1.1). They differ in "the degrees of force and liveliness, with which they strike upon the mind." Impressions are sensations, passions and emotions as they first appear; ideas are their faint images in thinking and reasoning. Both are simple or complex. Impressions are of sensation, arising from unknown causes, or of reflexion, the passions and desires, which arise largely from ideas (T 1.1.2.1). Hume restores "idea" to a narrower sense than Locke's, who used it for every object of thought. Sorting perceptions by vivacity makes feeling and thinking differ only in degree.

column1: What is the copy principle?
column2: The first principle of the system: "all our simple ideas in their first appearance are deriv'd from simple impressions, which are correspondent to them, and which they exactly represent" (T 1.1.1.7). The name is the scholars'. The evidence is experimental: every simple idea examined resembles an impression, and a man born blind has no ideas of colour (EHU 2.7). Complex ideas need not copy anything, since a golden mountain joins ideas we already have. The principle is a tool of criticism. When a term is suspected, "we need but enquire, from what impression is that supposed idea derived?" (EHU 2.9). Hume applies it to substance, necessary connexion and the self. He raises the missing shade of blue against it himself and keeps the maxim (EHU 2.8).

column1: What is the association of ideas?
column2: If ideas were "entirely loose and unconnected, chance alone wou'd join them" (T 1.1.4.1). Instead a "gentle force" guides the imagination. There are "only three principles of connexion among ideas, namely, Resemblance, Contiguity in time or place, and Cause or Effect" (EHU 3.2). A portrait leads to the person, a room to the next room, a wound to the pain. Hume compares association to gravity, "a kind of Attraction" in the mental world (T 1.1.4.6), and does not pretend to explain its causes. The Abstract calls these relations "the cement of the universe" (Abstract 35) and makes them the author's chief claim to be an inventor. Belief, the indirect passions and sympathy are all association at work.

column1: What is Hume's account of abstract ideas?
column2: Hume adopts Berkeley's account, calling it "one of the greatest and most valuable discoveries that has been made of late years in the republic of letters" (T 1.1.7.1). On it, "all general ideas are nothing but particular ones, annexed to a certain term, which gives them a more extensive signification." Locke had supposed an idea of a triangle neither equilateral, isosceles nor scalene. Hume denies it: every idea copies an impression, and every impression is fully determinate. He adds a mechanism. Hearing the word, we form the idea of one triangle, and a custom attached to the word stands ready to call up others. So a false general claim drawn from the one before us is checked (T 1.1.7.7–8). There is no indeterminate idea.

column1: What is the distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact?
column2: The Treatise lists seven philosophical relations and keeps four, those depending wholly on the ideas compared, as objects of knowledge (T 1.3.1.1–2). The Enquiry simplifies this into what later readers call Hume's fork: "All the objects of human reason or enquiry may naturally be divided into two kinds, to wit, Relations of Ideas, and Matters of Fact" (EHU 4.1). Relations of ideas, such as the theorems of geometry, are known "by the mere operation of thought." Of the second kind, "the contrary of every matter of fact is still possible" (EHU 4.2): that the sun will not rise tomorrow implies no contradiction. The fork closes the book as a rule for burning libraries (EHU 12.34). Whether it is the later analytic/synthetic distinction is disputed.

column1: What are Hume's two definitions of cause?
column2: Hume defines cause twice, taking the relation "either as a comparison of two ideas, or as an association betwixt them" (T 1.3.14.31). In the Enquiry a cause is "an object, followed by another, and where all the objects, similar to the first, are followed by objects similar to the second"; or "an object followed by another, and whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other" (EHU 7.29). The first is a regularity in objects, the second the mind's transition. Between them comes a counterfactual gloss that neither states. Hume concedes both are "drawn from circumstances foreign to the cause." J. A. Robinson (1962) judged them incompatible; Garrett reads them as agreeing for a suitably placed observer. The dispute is open.

column1: What is custom for Hume?
column2: Custom, or habit, is the principle that, after repeated constant conjunction, carries the mind from an impression to the idea of its usual attendant (EHU 5.5–6). It is not a social custom. It is the sceptical solution to induction: it explains the inference without justifying it. "Custom, then, is the great guide of human life. It is that principle alone, which renders our experience useful to us" (EHU 5.6). The Abstract is blunter: "'Tis not, therefore, reason, which is the guide of life, but custom" (Abstract 16). Custom is an original principle of human nature, and Hume does not try to explain it. It explains why a hundred instances move us when one does not (EHU 5.5), and it produces belief.

column1: What is belief, as force and vivacity?
column2: Belief adds no new idea to what is conceived; it changes the manner of conceiving. If it were an added idea, we could believe whatever we pleased (EHU 5.10). The Treatise defines it as "A lively idea related to or associated with a present impression" (T 1.3.7.5). The Enquiry piles up synonyms: "a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object, than what the imagination alone is ever able to attain" (EHU 5.12). The present impression passes its force along the customary relation, as a picture enlivens the idea of an absent friend (T 1.3.8.3). The Appendix stresses that "belief consists merely in a certain feeling or sentiment," not dependent on the will (T App. 2). Reid objected that vivid novels are not believed.

column1: What is the title principle?
column2: Book 1 of the Treatise ends in crisis: reason turned on itself would reduce belief to nothing, and Hume is cured by dinner, backgammon and friends (T 1.4.7.9). He returns to philosophy on a rule: "Where reason is lively, and mixes itself with some propensity, it ought to be assented to. Where it does not, it never can have any title to operate upon us" (T 1.4.7.11). Don Garrett (Cognition and Commitment in Hume's Philosophy, 1997) named it the title principle. Reasoning that rides on a natural propensity, such as causal inference about common life, may be followed. With the rules for judging causes (T 1.3.15), it is meant to filter out superstition. Whether that filter is principled is disputed.

column1: What is mitigated scepticism?
column2: The Enquiry contrasts two scepticisms. Pyrrhonian or excessive scepticism cannot be lived: "Nature is always too strong for principle," and "no durable good can ever result from it" (EHU 12.23). Mitigated or academical scepticism "may be both durable and useful." It is Pyrrhonism "corrected by common sense and reflection" (EHU 12.24). It leaves "a degree of doubt, and caution, and modesty" (EHU 12.24) and confines enquiry to subjects "best adapted to the narrow capacity of human understanding" (EHU 12.25). Philosophy survives as "the reflections of common life, methodized and corrected" (EHU 12.25). The opening section says the same: "Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man" (EHU 1.6).

column1: What is the bundle theory of the self?
column2: when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other (T 1.4.6.3). With no impression of a simple, unchanging self, there is no idea of one. People are "nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement" (T 1.4.6.4). The mind is "a kind of theatre," though we have no notion of the place where the scenes are played. We ascribe identity because resemblance and causation make the imagination's passage along the bundle smooth (T 1.4.6.6). Hume separates identity regarding thought from identity regarding the passions (T 1.4.6.5). The Appendix withdrew his confidence (T App. 10).

column1: What are direct and indirect passions?
column2: The passions are impressions of reflexion, also called secondary impressions (T 2.1.1.1), and are calm or violent. "By direct passions I understand such as arise immediately from good or evil, from pain or pleasure. By indirect such as proceed from the same principles, but by the conjunction of other qualities" (T 2.1.1.4). Desire, aversion, hope, fear, joy and grief are direct; pride and humility, love and hatred are indirect. An indirect passion has an object and a cause. The object of pride and humility is the self, that of love and hatred another person. The cause is a quality of something related, such as a fine house I own. The passion arises by a double relation of ideas and of impressions (T 2.1.5.5).

column1: What is sympathy for Hume?
column2: No quality of human nature is more remarkable, both in itself and in its consequences, than that propensity we have to sympathize with others (T 2.1.11.2). Sympathy is a mechanism of communication, not pity. I see the signs of another's feeling and form an idea of it, and "This idea is presently converted into an impression, and acquires such a degree of force and vivacity, as to become the very passion itself" (T 2.1.11.3). The idea draws its force from the ever-present impression of myself, through resemblance and nearness. So sympathy is strong toward those close to and like us and weak toward strangers. It spreads moral feeling, and sympathy with public interest is the source of our approval of justice (T 3.2.2.24).

column1: What is the general point of view?
column2: Sympathy varies with distance and resemblance, so moral judgment built on it would waver. Hume's correction: "we fix on some steady and general points of view; and always, in our thoughts, place ourselves in them, whatever may be our present situation" (T 3.3.1.15). We judge a character by its effects on those around it, not on ourselves. So "Virtue in rags is still virtue" (T 3.3.1.19): good qualities earn approval even when bad luck keeps them from doing good. The second Enquiry ties the standpoint to moral language. One who calls another vicious "must here, therefore, depart from his private and particular situation" (EPM 9.6). Adam Smith's impartial spectator develops the idea.

column1: What is the difference between natural and artificial virtues?
column2: Benevolence, generosity and clemency are natural virtues, approved without any social scheme. Justice, fidelity to promises and allegiance are artificial: "the sense of justice and injustice is not deriv'd from nature, but arises artificially, tho' necessarily from education, and human conventions" (T 3.2.1.17). Artificial is not arbitrary: "Mankind is an inventive species; and where an invention is obvious and absolutely necessary, it may as properly be said to be natural as any thing" (T 3.2.1.19). Justice arises from "the selfishness and confin'd generosity of men, along with the scanty provision nature has made for his wants" (T 3.2.2.18), through a convention without promise. Its laws are stability of possession, transference by consent and performance of promises (T 3.2.6.1).

column1: What is the moral sense for Hume?
column2: Morality "is more properly felt than judg'd of" (T 3.1.2.1). Reason finds no vice in a murder; you find it only when you "turn your reflection into your own breast" (T 3.1.1.26). "To have the sense of virtue, is nothing but to feel a satisfaction of a particular kind from the contemplation of a character" (T 3.1.2.3). Character is the object of evaluation, and actions count as its signs. Hume takes the phrase "moral sense" from Francis Hutcheson but explains the feeling by sympathy and utility. The second Enquiry gives reason more room: "reason and sentiment concur in almost all moral determinations" (EPM 1.9). Reason discovers objects as they stand; taste gilds or stains them "with the colours, borrowed from internal sentiment" (EPM App. 1.21).

column1: What is Hume's standard of taste?
column2: Of the Standard of Taste (1757) grants the sceptical premise: "Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them" ("Of the Standard of Taste" 7). It still finds a standard, in the general principles shown by works admired across ages, and in the qualified judge. "Strong sense, united to delicate sentiment, improved by practice, perfected by comparison, and cleared of all prejudice" makes the true critic, and "the joint verdict of such, wherever they are to be found, is the true standard of taste and beauty" ("Of the Standard of Taste" 23). The illustration, from Don Quixote, is Sancho's two kinsmen, who taste leather and iron in a hogshead of wine; a key on a leather thong lies at the bottom. Critics see a circle here.

column1: Why does Hume found government on opinion?
column2: Of the First Principles of Government (1741) asks how the few rule the many. "As Force is always on the side of the governed, the governors have nothing to support them but opinion. It is therefore, on opinion only that government is founded" ("Of the First Principles of Government" 1). "Of the Original Contract" (1748) attacks the Whig doctrine that government rests on consent. Present governments began mostly in conquest or usurpation, and tacit consent by residence is a fiction: a poor peasant who knows no foreign language has no free choice to leave ("Of the Original Contract" 24). Allegiance and fidelity both rest on the interests of society, so "We gain nothing by resolving the one into the other" ("Of the Original Contract" 36).
